title: CPU Datapath and the Single-Cycle Processor
subtitle: What really happens inside the CPU when an instruction executes.

references.title: The Processor
references.topics: Introduction; logic design conventions; building a datapath; a simple implementation scheme (ALU control, main control unit, operation of the datapath)

objectives: Name the datapath components and what each one does
Build the single-cycle datapath step by step
Follow add, lw, sw and beq through the datapath
Read the control signals for each instruction type
Calculate the clock cycle time of a single-cycle processor

steps.question: You wrote `lw $t0, 8($s1)`. Which wires carry which bits, and who tells each wire what to do?
clues: The instruction travels through a **datapath** of memories, registers and an ALU.
A **control unit** decides which paths are used.
In the simplest design **one whole instruction finishes in one clock cycle**.

notes.explain: Let students guess before revealing the clues.
Read the objectives aloud; they return in the learning report.

steps.title: Datapath and control

left.title: Datapath
items: The hardware that **holds and moves data**

right.title: Control
items: The logic that **tells** the datapath what to do
A control unit that reads the instruction and sets signals

steps.why: Every processor is split in two: parts that do the work, and parts that direct it.
steps.real: The same idea applies to a car: the engine and wheels are the datapath; the driver and pedals are the control.

explainAgain.beginner: Think of an orchestra: the instruments are the datapath, the conductor is the control.

notes.explain: Reveal one row at a time. Ask the class why we need two adders and an ALU.

steps.title: Build it up

steps.text: The **program counter** holds the address of the instruction. It addresses the **instruction memory**.
Fields of the instruction name the registers to read in the **register file**; a multiplexer picks the destination register.
The **ALU** operates on register data, or on register data and an immediate chosen by a multiplexer.
The 16-bit immediate is **sign-extended** to 32 bits so it can be an ALU input.
**Data memory** is read or written for loads and stores; a multiplexer chooses what is written back to the register file.
The PC normally advances by 4 to the next instruction.
For branches, a second adder computes the **branch target** and the ALU's Zero output helps choose the next PC.
The **control unit** reads the opcode and sets every multiplexer and memory control signal.

steps.why: Each click adds one group of components. The complete datapath is never given at once.

steps.question: Which component holds the address of the instruction being executed?
steps.why: The program counter (PC) holds that address.
feedback: The register file holds data, not the instruction address.
Data memory is for loads and stores.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Match each component with its job.

pairs.b: Holds the address of the current instruction
Does the arithmetic and the comparisons

steps.why: Each component has one clear role.

steps.question: Why does the single-cycle design need separate instruction memory and data memory?
options: One instruction needs to fetch itself and also read or write data in the same cycle
Instructions are 16 bits and data is 32 bits
Memory cannot store instructions and data together
steps.why: In one cycle both the instruction fetch and a load or store happen, so two memories are needed.
feedback: Both are 32 bits wide in MIPS.
A real memory can hold both; the problem is using it twice in one cycle.
Two memories cost more, not less.

questions.q: What is the difference between datapath and control?
questions.a: The datapath holds and moves data; control decides what the datapath does.

questions.q: What does the sign-extend unit do?
questions.a: Extends the 16-bit immediate to 32 bits, keeping its sign.

questions.q: Why is there a multiplexer in front of the ALU?
questions.a: To choose between a register value and the immediate.

steps.title: Four steps for every instruction

nodes.label: Fetch
nodes.note: The instruction is read and PC + 4 is computed.

nodes.label: Decode
nodes.note: Register fields select registers; the control unit sets signals.

nodes.label: Execute
nodes.note: Compute a result, an address or a comparison.

nodes.label: Memory and write back
nodes.note: Loads read memory, stores write it; results go to a register.

steps.why: All instructions share fetch and decode; they differ in what happens afterwards.
steps.real: Debuggers that "step" through code show these same stages.

steps.title: Instruction, data, ALU, result

items: **Instruction** moves from instruction memory to the register file, sign extender and control unit
**Data** moves from the registers (and memory) toward the ALU
The **ALU** produces a result, an address or a Zero flag
The **result** goes back to a register, to memory, or to the PC

steps.why: Following these four flows tells you what any instruction does.

steps.question: For `lw $t0, 8($s1)`, which component computes the memory address?

reveal.text: The ALU adds the base register $s1 and the sign-extended offset 8. The result is the address sent to data memory.

steps.result: The ALU is used for addresses as well as arithmetic.

steps.title: Follow an instruction

blocks.title: Follow one instruction through the datapath

steps.text: The complete single-cycle datapath. Pick an instruction scenario and press Play or Step.
**Fetch**: the PC addresses the instruction memory and the instruction is read.
**Decode**: the control unit sets the signals for an R-type instruction; registers $s1 and $s2 are read.
**Execute**: the ALU adds the two register values.
**Write back**: the ALU result (not memory data) goes to the destination register $t0.
**Next instruction**: PC + 4 becomes the new PC.
**Fetch** the load instruction.
**Decode**: read the base register $s1; sign-extend the offset 8.
**Execute**: the ALU adds the base and the offset to form the **address**.
**Memory access**: data memory is read at that address.
**Write back**: the loaded value goes to $t0 (here MemtoReg = 1, RegDst = 0).
**Fetch** the store instruction.
**Decode**: read $s1 (base) and $t0 (the value to store); sign-extend the offset.
**Execute**: compute the address base + offset.
**Memory access**: the register value is **written** to data memory. Nothing is written back to a register.
**Fetch** the branch instruction.
**Decode**: read the two registers to compare; sign-extend the offset.
**Execute**: the ALU subtracts the registers. If they are equal the result is zero and the **Zero** output is 1.
At the same time the **branch adder** computes PC + 4 + (offset × 4).
Branch AND Zero selects the branch target as the **next PC** (PCSrc = 1).

steps.why: Run add, lw, sw and beq. For each one, watch which components light up and which stay idle.

steps.title: The same instructions in the simulator

blocks.title: lw, add, sw, beq
blocks.program:
lui $s1, 0x1001
lw $t0, 8($s1)
add $t1, $t0, $t0
sw $t1, 12($s1)
beq $t0, $t1, end
end:
blocks.hint: lw reads 21 from address 0x10010008, add doubles it, sw stores 42 at 0x1001000C, and beq does not branch because 21 ≠ 42.

steps.why: Every line here follows the datapath path you have just seen.

steps.question: `add $t0, $s1, $s2` runs through the datapath. Does it use the data memory?
options: Only if the result is negative

reveal.text: R-type instructions never touch data memory. Their result goes straight from the ALU back to the register file through the MemtoReg multiplexer.

steps.result: Only lw and sw use data memory.

steps.title: Mini challenge
steps.prompt: Put the steps of `lw` in order.
items: Fetch the instruction using the PC
Read the base register and sign-extend the offset
The ALU adds base and offset
Data memory reads the word at that address
Write the word into the destination register
steps.why: Each step needs the output of the one before it.

steps.title: Find the mistake
steps.prompt: One statement about instruction execution is wrong. Click it.
lines: 1. lw uses the ALU to compute an address.
2. sw writes a register value into data memory.
3. beq writes its result to a register.
4. add does not use data memory.
steps.explain: beq compares two registers and may change the PC; it writes no register.
steps.fix: beq does not write a register.

steps.title: Eight control signals

head: Signal
Meaning when 1 (or the other value)
rows: Destination register is rd (R-type); 0 means rt (lw, addi)
ALU second input is the immediate; 0 means a register
Write memory data to the register; 0 means the ALU result
The instruction is a branch (used with Zero to choose the next PC)
2 bits: tells the ALU control what operation to select

steps.why: Each signal is one multiplexer select or one write-enable, so eight signals steer the whole datapath.
steps.real: Changing the instruction set means changing this table, not the datapath, in many designs.

steps.title: Signal values per instruction
steps.why: X means "don't care": the value does not affect the result because nothing is written there.
steps.real: This table is stored as the logic of the control unit, usually a few dozen gates.

mistake.wrong: sw has RegWrite = 1 because it uses a register.
mistake.right: sw only reads registers; it writes memory, so RegWrite = 0 and MemWrite = 1.

deeper.text: The 2-bit ALUOp (00 add, 01 subtract, 10 look at funct) lets a small ALU control choose the final 4-bit ALU operation.

steps.title: The branch decision

terms.note: take the branch only for a branch instruction whose comparison gave zero
the offset is shifted left 2 because instructions are 4 bytes

steps.why: beq subtracts its two registers; if the result is zero (Zero = 1) they are equal and the branch is taken.
steps.real: The same logic decides every if statement at the hardware level.

mistake.wrong: The branch target is PC plus the offset.
mistake.right: It is PC + 4 plus the offset times 4.

steps.question: Which control signals are 1 for `sw`?

reveal.text: sw adds a base and an offset (**ALUSrc = 1**) and writes data memory (**MemWrite = 1**). It writes no register (RegWrite = 0).

steps.result: RegDst and MemtoReg are don't care for sw.

steps.question: `beq` is at 0x00400020 with offset 3 and the registers are equal. Where does the next instruction come from?
feedback: That uses PC + 12 instead of PC + 4 + 12.

steps.statement: The control unit changes its signals depending on the opcode of the current instruction.
steps.why: That is its whole job: opcode in, control signals out.

steps.title: The slowest instruction sets the clock

items: Every instruction takes **one clock cycle**, so the cycle must be long enough for the slowest instruction
The slowest is usually **lw**: it uses every component in sequence
The longest sequence of components is the **critical path**

blocks.text: The delays below are **illustrative**, chosen to make the arithmetic clear. Real values depend on the technology.

steps.why: If the clock is too fast for lw, the load would not finish and the processor would produce wrong results.
steps.real: Processor designers shorten the critical path to raise the clock speed.

steps.title: Calculate the clock period

results.label: Time wasted by an R-type instruction

steps.why: With the default delays lw takes 800 ps, so the clock period is 800 ps (1,250 MHz). An R-type instruction needs only 600 ps, so 200 ps are wasted. Make the ALU slower and watch the period change.

steps.question: With these delays the clock period is 800 ps. If the data memory were made twice as fast (100 ps), what would the new period be?

reveal.text: lw becomes 200 + 100 + 200 + 100 + 100 = **700 ps**, and it is still the slowest.

steps.result: Check that lw is still the critical path: R-type is 600 ps and sw is 600 ps.

steps.title: Think, pair, share
steps.prompt: If only 25% of instructions are lw, why must every instruction wait for the lw time?
steps.answer: The clock period is the same for all instructions and the hardware cannot know in advance which instruction comes next, so the clock must be long enough for the slowest. That wastes time on faster instructions, which is the weakness the multi-cycle design (Class 11) and pipelining (Class 12) address.

steps.title: Discussion
steps.question: Single-cycle has CPI = 1. Why is it still not the fastest design?
ideas: The long clock period slows every instruction.
Hardware is duplicated: two memories and three adders cannot be shared.
Faster instructions waste time waiting for the slowest.
Shorter cycles with more of them can finish the average instruction sooner.

steps.question: Name the main components of the single-cycle datapath.
steps.answer: PC, instruction memory, register file, sign extender, ALU, data memory, multiplexers, adders and the control unit.
steps.solution: These nine are all in the diagram you built.

steps.question: Which components does `add $t0, $s1, $s2` use? Which does it skip?
steps.answer: Uses PC, instruction memory, register file (read and write), ALU and the control unit; skips data memory.
steps.solution: R-type results go straight from the ALU back to the register file.
steps.hint: Does add read or write memory?

steps.question: Give the eight control signals for `lw`.
steps.answer: RegDst 0, ALUSrc 1, MemtoReg 1, RegWrite 1, MemRead 1, MemWrite 0, Branch 0, ALUOp 00.
steps.solution: lw writes rt (RegDst 0), uses the immediate (ALUSrc 1), takes data from memory (MemtoReg 1), writes a register (RegWrite 1), reads memory (MemRead 1) and adds (ALUOp 00).
steps.hint: What does lw read, and where does the result go?
steps.mistake: Setting RegDst to 1 because lw writes a register.

steps.question: The delays are IM 200, register read 100, ALU 300, DM 200, register write 100 ps. What is the clock period?
steps.solution: lw = 200 + 100 + 300 + 200 + 100 = 900 ps; R-type = 700 ps; the longest path is lw.
steps.hint: Add up the components on the lw path.

steps.question: `addi $t0, $s1, 5` is added to the processor. Give the control signals.
steps.answer: RegDst 0, ALUSrc 1, MemtoReg 0, RegWrite 1, MemRead 0, MemWrite 0, Branch 0, ALUOp 00.
steps.solution: addi writes rt (RegDst 0), uses the immediate (ALUSrc 1), writes the ALU result (MemtoReg 0), writes a register (RegWrite 1), does not touch memory and does not branch. The ALU just adds (ALUOp 00).
steps.mistake: Setting MemtoReg to 1 (that is for lw).
steps.title: Exam practice: signal table

steps.question: Delays: IM 250, register read 150, ALU 200, DM 300, register write 150 ps. Find the lw time, the R-type time, the clock period, and the time an R-type wastes.
steps.answer: lw 1050 ps; R-type 750 ps; clock period 1050 ps; R-type wastes 300 ps.
steps.mistake: Using the R-type time as the clock period.
steps.title: Exam practice: numerical

steps.question: `beq` is at 0x00400020 and its offset is 3. The registers are equal. What is the next PC, and what is PCSrc?
steps.solution: Branch = 1 and Zero = 1 give PCSrc = 1. Target = 0x00400020 + 4 + 3 × 4 = 0x00400030.
steps.title: Exam practice: branch target

steps.question: Explain why a single-cycle processor needs two memories and why its clock is set by lw.
steps.answer: In one cycle the processor must both fetch the instruction and, for lw or sw, access data, so it needs an instruction memory and a data memory (a single memory could be used once per cycle). The clock period must cover the slowest instruction: lw uses all five steps in sequence, so it defines the critical path, and faster instructions waste the difference.
steps.solution: A strong answer links one cycle per instruction to both the duplicated hardware and the long clock.
steps.mistake: Saying the clock is set by the average instruction.
steps.title: Exam practice: conceptual
What you should remember
remember: The datapath moves data; the control unit sets the signals that steer it.
Components: PC, instruction memory, register file, sign extend, ALU, data memory, multiplexers, adders.
Every instruction: fetch, decode, execute, then memory and write back as needed.
lw uses every component; add skips data memory; sw writes memory but no register; beq writes nothing.
Control signals: RegDst, ALUSrc, MemtoReg, RegWrite, MemRead, MemWrite, Branch, ALUOp.
PCSrc = Branch AND Zero; target = PC + 4 + offset × 4.
Clock period = the slowest instruction (lw); other instructions waste time.

mistakes.wrong: The control unit does the arithmetic.
mistakes.right: The ALU does; control sets signals.

mistakes.wrong: The clock is set by the average instruction.
mistakes.right: It is set by the slowest, usually lw.

mistakes.wrong: The branch target is PC plus the offset.

steps.title: One-minute summary
steps.summary: A single-cycle processor finishes each instruction in one clock cycle through one datapath: PC, instruction memory, register file, ALU, data memory, multiplexers and adders. The control unit decodes the opcode into eight control signals. Because the clock must fit the slowest instruction (lw), simple instructions waste time and hardware is duplicated, which leads to the multi-cycle design.
